beats.beat: Harker receives Phoebe in the cold front hall, will not let her see Miss Fairfax, and hands her an old gown to take the measurements from instead.
Phoebe tells him plainly that a tradeswoman is owed the same civility as any customer, and he answers that her business is the cloth, not his household's affairs.
Through a part-opened door Phoebe glimpses Augusta Fairfax in unrelieved black, quietly weeping over a packet of letters, plainly grieved and not raving.
Harker abruptly cancels the order, presses payment well above its worth into Phoebe's hand, and shows her out, leaving her certain she has been paid to keep silent.

turn.note: Chapter ends on Phoebe's flat conclusion that she has been paid for silence, which sets up her account-tracing in chapter 3.

generic_prose.quote: in the way of a person who has been at it some while and expects to be at it longer
generic_prose.replace_with: a concrete physical detail of Augusta's grief — the letters crushed in her fist, a particular gesture — rather than a generalised description of weeping that could belong to any crying character in any story

trope_note: Delivers the madwoman misdirection straight (reader sees grief, not madness, before the parish does) and advances enemies-of-manner through the Harker/Phoebe clash; the secret benefactor trope is seeded by the suspicious over-payment.
fixes: Replace 'in the way of a person who has been at it some while and expects to be at it longer' with one concrete physical detail specific to Augusta.
Consider trimming the opening sentence's trailing clause slightly, though it currently holds only two coordinated members and is acceptable as is.
